PMID:31666018.setting: University Hospital of North Norway, Tromsø; Level 1 trauma centre, patients with trauma team activation registered in the Norwegian national trauma registry
PMID:31666018.standard: Expert coder group consensus reference standard using the AIS 2005 Update 2008 manual (review of all EHR data and reinterpretation of all imaging); no target stated

cycle1.dates: Patients admitted in 2015; reference standard coding February 2016 to March 2017
cycle1.result: 582 AIS codes in the registry vs 766 in the reference standard. All injuries concordantly coded in 62 (43.1%) patients. 166 missing codes in 71 (49.3%) patients, mostly AIS 1, chiefly EHR information overlooked by coders. 157 discordant codes in 74 (51.4%) patients, mainly head injuries and extremity fractures. Median ISS (9) and NISS (12) identical in registry and reference standard; ISS changed in 52 (36.1%) patients; no significant difference on Bland–Altman regression (ISS p = 0.078, NISS p = 0.656).

PMID:31666018.other_findings: A software error in registry data retrieval omitted 46 duplicate codes and was corrected by the registry; the authors trained trauma physicians in AIS coding and proposed adding coding review to the monthly trauma audit, but no re-measurement is reported.

PMID:35031854.setting: Addenbrooke's Major Trauma Unit, Cambridge University Hospitals; major trauma centre, open talus fractures in skeletally mature patients
PMID:35031854.standard: BOAST 4 guidelines for open fractures (e.g. prophylactic antibiotics within one hour of injury, definitive soft tissue coverage within 72 h, orthoplastic involvement, debridement); no target stated

cycle1.result: 15 open talus fractures in 14 patients. 100% had orthoplastic involvement, initial saline-soaked gauze and occlusive film dressing, functional recovery and rehabilitation advice, and recorded debridement; 60% had debridement using fasciotomy lines. Only 27% received prophylactic antibiotics within one hour of injury and only 27% achieved definitive soft tissue coverage within 72 h (mean 9.7 days in the 7 needing coverage).

PMID:35031854.other_findings: Mainly a cohort comparison: no significant difference between ORIF and tibiocalcaneal fusion in EQ-5D-5L (p = 0.13), FAAM-ADL (p = 0.20), FAAM-Sport (p = 0.34) or infection rate (p = 0.55); deep infection occurred in 7 cases (47%).

PMID:36106695.setting: National Joint Registry (England, Wales, Northern Ireland, Isle of Man, Guernsey); national data quality audit of all NHS and independent sector arthroplasty units
PMID:36106695.standard: Compliance of NJR entries validated against each unit's Patient Administration System; target 95% or higher compliance

cycle1.result: Baseline average organisation-level compliance 92.64% (92.6%), with over 7,000 cases in provider data but missing from the NJR; 9.7% of revision hips missing vs 5.6% of primaries, and 9.8% of revision knees vs 5.1% of primaries.

PMID:36106695.intervention: Annual bidirectional data quality audit cycle: statements of missing cases sent to units for retrospective entry, named data quality lead per unit, data completeness awards and tariff top-up targets, audit reports with action plans to CEOs and clinical leads, unit visits, communications and user guides, and a semi-automated upload platform from 2018.

cycle2.result: Baseline compliance rose year-on-year to 96.0% in 2018/19, reaching 97.9% overall after closure of the audit cycle; 76.4% of units achieved >95% compliance (61.5% of units achieved ≥95% on first run of the 2018/19 audit). 314 units completed the 2018/19 audit.

PMID:36106695.other_findings: Intermediate unit-level baseline compliance was 91.78% (2015/16), 92.46% (2016/17) and 94.12% (2017/18), with missing cases falling from 11,285 to 8,670; a persistent gap remained between primary and revision procedures.

PMID:40441733.topic: Suspected cauda equina time to MRI
PMID:40441733.setting: Medway Maritime Hospital, Gillingham; district general hospital emergency department without on-site emergency spinal surgery
PMID:40441733.standard: GIRFT National Suspected CES Pathway 2023: emergency MRI within 4 hours of request; local SMART aim of median under 4 hours from ED attendance to MRI within 1 year

cycle1.result: Median time from ED presentation to MRI 5.9 hours (IQR 4.9–14.7) although median MRI request to scan was 1.7 hours (IQR 1.1–3.7), meeting the GIRFT target; 8% of patients incorrectly sent to the GP-led MEDOCC service. At PDSA 1: 38% of MRIs unnecessary, 0.5 CES MRIs/day, time to analgesia 5.3 hours (IQR 3.8–7.0), 9% inappropriately triaged to MEDOCC.

PMID:40441733.intervention: Three PDSA cycles (July 2023 to January 2024): CES working group and trust-level awareness; new locally adapted SOP based on the GIRFT pathway with CES-specific shorter MRI sequences; ED triage and assessment posters, board round, grand round and senior-led teaching. Planned extension of MRI hours was not achieved.

cycle2.dates: PDSA 3, cycles run July 2023 to January 2024
cycle2.result: Approximately 27 patients per cycle. Median ED presentation to MRI 5.7 hours (IQR 4.1–14.3), primary aim not met; GIRFT 4-hour request-to-scan target met in all cycles. Unnecessary MRIs fell from 38% to 18%, CES MRIs 0.5/day to 0.4/day, time to analgesia 5.3 to 4.2 hours (IQR 2.7–7.0), and inappropriate MEDOCC referrals 9% to 0%.

PMID:40441733.other_findings: Time to MRI rose to 9.9 hours in PDSA 2 amid ED pressures and industrial action; 43/81 patients presented at times making same-day MRI unlikely because scanners ran only until 20:00, and by PDSA 3 attendance to MRI request was still a median 3.9 hours.

PMID:25410899.setting: Arthroplasty Clinical Outcomes Registry NSW (ACORN); two major hospitals (A and B) in New South Wales
PMID:25410899.standard: Benchmark of 95.0% for data completeness and accuracy against reabstracted medical record data

cycle1.dates: Surgery in 2012/2013 (first six months of data submission)
cycle1.result: Completeness 99.0% (1259/1272) Hospital A and 99.3% (1589/1600) Hospital B; accuracy 94.0% (2159/2296) Hospital A and 96.1% (2444/2542) Hospital B. 57.1% (28/49) of variables met the 95% accuracy benchmark in A and 74.5% (38/51) in B. Registry captured 93.5% (660/706) of eligible patients.

PMID:25410899.other_findings: Most accuracy discrepancies were in comorbidity (medical history) data, e.g. hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and GIT; only 10.2% (A) and 8.0% (B) of records were entirely error-free. 100 records were sampled; one from Hospital A was excluded.

PMID:29859072.setting: Advanced practice physiotherapist triage services in orthopaedic and rheumatology clinics at 16 major acute hospitals; national database, with re-referral pilot at St Vincent's University Hospital, Dublin

cycle1.result: 13,981 new patients seen by 22 APPs; median wait 167 days (IQR 91–316). APPs made autonomous decisions at 77.2% of appointments; 18.1% required onward referral to orthopaedic or rheumatology consultants; physiotherapy referral 41.5%, investigations 29.3%, injections 4.1%, surgical listing 2.4%. Of 184 patients managed without consultant referral, 12 (6.5%) were re-referred within one year and 20 (10.9%) within two years.

PMID:29859072.other_findings: Knee (23%), lumbar spine (22%) and shoulder (15%) were the commonest presentations; 70% of re-referred patients had no change in management.

PMID:26313924.topic: Fragility fracture recording and bone protection
PMID:26313924.setting: 12 general practices in Crawley, south-east England; primary care, community-based fracture liaison nurse pilot
PMID:26313924.standard: Anticipated pay-for-performance (QOF/Directed Enhanced Service) osteoporosis indicators: register of patients with fragility fracture, and treatment with a bone-sparing agent in those aged 50–74 with confirmed osteoporosis and in those aged 75 and over with a fragility fracture

cycle1.result: Females 50–74 (n=13,519) and ≥75 (n=4,883). Bone-sparing agent in those aged 50–74 with fragility fracture and confirmed osteoporosis 47.9% (23/48); in those ≥75 with fragility fracture 39.5% (118/181). Fragility fracture recorded 8.8% (15/171) aged 50–74 and 0.8% (65/8110) aged ≥75.

PMID:26313924.intervention: Introduction of a community-based fracture liaison nurse who reviewed the practice population meeting the inclusion criteria.

cycle2.result: Bone-sparing agent 84.0% (42/50) aged 50–74 and 70.5% (222/316) aged ≥75 (p<0.001). Fragility fracture recorded 14% (25/178) aged 50–74 (p=0.168) and 2.3% (199/8702) aged ≥75 (p<0.001).

PMID:26313924.other_findings: Recording of smoking and BMI roughly doubled, but DXA scan recording fell (e.g. 2.5% to 1.4% in those ≥75); less deprived patients were more likely to receive DXA scans and more deprived patients bone-sparing agents.

PMID:31276053.setting: Emergency department, City Hospitals Sunderland NHS Foundation Trust; district general hospital, adults 16 and over
PMID:31276053.standard: Royal College of Emergency Medicine guidelines on time to shoulder dislocation reduction (2-hour RCEM clinical standard of 75% for initial attempt at reduction)

cycle1.result: Average triage to confirmed shoulder reduction X-ray 2 hours 25 min (range 1 h 14 min to 5 h 3 min); triage to discharge 3 hours 22 min (range 1 h 46 min to 6 h 39 min); 57% (17/30) sedated for reduction.

PMID:31276053.intervention: Shoulder Reduction Bench (modified Oxford Chair) introduced with three PDSA cycles: training of emergency nurse practitioners, written protocol and flowchart on the intranet, and an online training video.

cycle2.dates: 6 months after project launch (March to September)
cycle2.result: Average triage to confirmed reduction X-ray 1 hour 54 min (31 min, 21% reduction); triage to discharge 2 hours 30 min (52 min, 26% reduction); 18% (7) sedated, a 68% reduction.

PMID:31276053.other_findings: The protocol was not followed in 2 cases (5%, both consultants) and adherence was unclear in 2 more; after restricting use to protocol criteria there were no further complications.

PMID:39845066.topic: Hip fracture follow-up after internal fixation
PMID:39845066.setting: Midland Regional Hospital Tullamore; Irish tertiary referral trauma unit, fracture clinic follow-up after DHS or intramedullary nail

cycle1.result: 428 outpatient appointments (mean 1.6 per patient); mean 1.13 inpatient and 1.54 outpatient radiographs per patient. 16 (5.8%) had abnormal radiographs and 8 (2.9%) underwent revision surgery; 15/16 (94%) with complications were symptomatic. DNA rate 13.1% costing €1,400; total follow-up cost €92,252 over 3 years.

PMID:39845066.other_findings: Cost analysis rather than audit; the authors propose selective and virtual follow-up and note that Irish integrated care pathway guidance advises routine follow-up 6 weeks after DHS or IM nail fixation.

PMID:29392102.setting: Galway University Hospital fracture clinics; tertiary care hospital, consultant-led
PMID:29392102.standard: BOAST Guideline 7 (fracture clinic services), assessed with a patient questionnaire adapted from the RCSI SWOPS questionnaire; no target stated

cycle1.result: Average wait for appointment 3.55 days (85 hours); wait to see doctor in clinic 56.81 minutes; doctors rated excellent 75%; X-ray facilities inadequate 34.7%; waiting area inadequate 44.93%; overall experience excellent 50.72%.

PMID:29392102.intervention: Changed fracture clinic appointment rotation, increased doctors on site, ensured patients returning from X-ray saw the same doctor, optimised follow-up X-ray process and increased waiting area seating from about 40 to 50; findings on X-ray location passed to management.

cycle2.result: Average wait for appointment 3.21 days (77.04 hours); wait to see doctor 52.55 minutes; doctors rated excellent 73.9%; X-ray facilities inadequate 32.79%; waiting area inadequate 41.49%; overall experience excellent 53.55%.

PMID:29392102.other_findings: The X-ray department remained a five-minute, partly outdoor walk from the clinic and waiting area ratings stayed poor; the year of data collection is not stated.

PMID:9607659.setting: Six accident and emergency departments; regional study led by the Northern Ireland Plastic and Maxillofacial Unit, Ulster Hospital

cycle1.result: Isolated hand or wrist injuries made up 6.6% of attendances; male:female ratio 2.2:1; mean age 26.4 years (men) and 29.2 years (women); 16.3% caused by falls, 15% by sport and 7% work/machinery related; 13.3% referred to specialities for further treatment.

PMID:9607659.other_findings: Abstract only; right and left hands were injured almost equally, with the dominant hand more often injured.
